name: Uyghur kingdoms of Qocho and Ganzhou
summary: Kingdoms founded by Uyghurs who fled after their steppe khaganate fell (840); in the Turfan oases they built a Buddhist and Manichaean culture of wall paintings and manuscripts, later submitting to the Mongols (1209).

location.value: Turfan oasis and the Gansu corridor (north-west China).

terrain.value: Desert oases in the Turfan basin and Hexi corridor, below high mountains.

climate.value: Very dry, with extreme heat in summer and cold winters.

resources.value: Irrigated grapes, cotton and grain, along with Silk Road trade.

disasters.value: Droughts and the failure of irrigation canals.

urbanisation.value: Qocho (Gaochang, near Turpan) was the winter capital and Beshbalik the summer capital.

disease.value: Plague and epidemics carried along trade routes.

migration.value: Uyghurs fled from Mongolia after the khaganate fell in 840.

economicBase.value: Oasis farming, crafts and trade on the Silk Road.

tradeRoutes.value: The Silk Road linked Qocho and Ganzhou to China, Persia and India.

wealth.value: Trade brought wealth to the oasis cities.

moneyAndTax.value: Coins and cloth, with taxes on caravans.

inequality.value: Ruling clans above commoner herders and slaves.

governmentType.value: Kingdoms ruled by an iduq-qut (“holy fortune”); Qocho had strong Chinese Buddhist and Tocharian influences.

keyRulers.value: Barchuk Art Tegin, the iduq-qut who threw off Qara Khitai rule and submitted to Genghis Khan (1209).

succession.value: Royal family, with the title idikut at Qocho.

institutions.value: Buddhist monasteries and a royal court.

majorWars.value: Ganzhou taken by the Tangut Western Xia (1028).

territoryChange.value: Lost Aksu, Tumshuk and Kucha to the Kara-Khanids (by 1096); later became part of the Chagatai Khanate.

alliancesRivals.value: A vassal of the Qara Khitai from 1128; fought the Kara-Khanids; joined the Mongols in 1209.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled horsemanship and metalwork.

scienceEducation.value: Monastic learning and translation of Buddhist and Manichaean texts.

openness.value: Open to trade and alliances with settled empires.

communicationTransport.value: Camel caravans carried goods and ideas.

religion.value: Buddhism (over fifty temples at Qocho), Manichaeism (its temples became Buddhist in 1008), Church of the East Christianity, and a growing Muslim community.

languageWriting.value: Old Uyghur, written in a script adopted from the Sogdians.

artsArchitecture.value: The Bezeklik cave temples, sponsored by the Uyghurs, with murals of Uyghur Buddhist patrons.

socialStructure.value: Turkic, Tocharian, Chinese and Sogdian peoples were absorbed into the kingdom.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Uyghur identity based on language, religion and the oasis way of life.

dailyLife.value: Oasis families grew grapes and grain, living in mud-brick houses.

neighbours.value: China, Tibet, Western Xia and the Karakhanids.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism, Manichaeism and Nestorian Christianity coexisted under royal tolerance.

riseSignals.value: After the Uyghur Khaganate fell (840), Uyghurs founded the Kingdom of Qocho (843) and, in the Hexi Corridor, the Ganzhou kingdom.

peakPeriod.value: The 900s–1000s, when Buddhist art and trade flourished.

outcome.value: Became part of the Mongol Chagatai Khanate; its people later became Muslim.

overallCertainty.value: Known mostly from Byzantine, Chinese, Arab and Persian writers and from archaeology; numbers are estimates.
